title: Signal Conditioning
description: Bridges turn resistance changes into voltages; instrumentation amplifiers boost them while rejecting common-mode noise; filters remove what is left.

study.title: Wheatstone bridge
study.body:
Two voltage dividers fed by the same excitation $V_{ex}$; the output is the **difference** $v_{ab}$ of their midpoints. The bridge is **balanced** ($v_{ab} = 0$) when the ratios match: $R_1R_x = R_2R_3$.
With one active sensor (quarter bridge, all arms nominally $R$) a small change $\Delta R$ gives $v_{ab} \approx -\frac{V_{ex}}{4}\frac{\Delta R}{R}$; two active arms double it, four (full bridge) give $V_{ex}\,\Delta R/R$.

study.title: Differential and common-mode signals
study.body:
Two input voltages $v_1$ and $v_2$ split into a **differential** part (usually the signal) and a **common-mode** part (often a large, unwanted offset or noise, e.g. $V_{ex}/2$ at a bridge output).
A real differential amplifier responds a little to the common mode: $v_o = A_d v_d + A_{cm}v_{cm}$. The common-mode rejection ratio $\text{CMRR} = 20\log_{10}|A_d/A_{cm}|$ (dB) measures how well it ignores it.

study.title: Instrumentation amplifier
study.body:
Three op amps: two non-inverting input buffers and a unity-gain difference amplifier. Both inputs go straight into op-amp + inputs, so the **input resistance is very high** for both. The single resistor $R_G$ sets the gain. A pure common-mode input makes no current flow in $R_G$, so the first stage passes $v_{cm}$ with gain 1 while amplifying $v_d$: excellent CMRR without needing matched sensor resistances.
(Hambley writes the gain as $1 + R_2/R_1$ with $R_G = 2R_1$.)

study.title: Difference amplifier
study.body: One op amp and four resistors. With $R_4/R_3 = R_2/R_1$ the output depends only on $v_1 - v_2$. Drawbacks: the input resistance is only about $R_1$ to $R_3 + R_4$, the sensor's own resistance adds to $R_1$/$R_3$, and any resistor mismatch $\delta$ lets common mode through: CMRR $\approx (1 + R_2/R_1)/\delta$.

study.title: Filtering noise
study.body: After amplification, a low-pass filter removes noise above the band of interest and acts as the **anti-alias** filter before the ADC. A first-order RC low-pass ($f_c = 1/2\pi RC$) passes signals well below $f_c$ and falls by 20 dB/decade above it (−3 dB at $f_c$). Higher-order active filters (e.g. Butterworth) fall faster: $20n$ dB/decade. Drag $f_c$ and the order $n$ (Butterworth). The readout is the attenuation at 10 kHz, the folding frequency of a 20 kS/s ADC: for the same cutoff, each extra order adds 20 dB per decade.

steps.title: The Wheatstone bridge
steps.body: A sensor's resistance change is turned into a voltage with a **bridge**: two dividers across the excitation $V_{ex}$. The output $v_{ab}$ is the difference of the two midpoint voltages, so it is zero when the bridge is **balanced** and changes when the sensor $R_x$ changes.

steps.prompt: In the bridge, $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} and $R_3$ = {{R3|Ω}}. For which value of $R_x$ is the bridge balanced ($v_{ab} = 0$)?
steps.explanation: Balanced when both dividers give the same fraction: $\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} = \frac{R_x}{R_3+R_x}$, i.e. $\frac{R_x}{R_3} = \frac{R_2}{R_1}$. So $R_x = R_3\frac{R_2}{R_1}$ = {{R3|Ω}} × {{R2|Ω}} / {{R1|Ω}} = **{{R2*R3/R1|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: Find the bridge output $v_{ab} = v_a - v_b$.

steps.title: Differential and common mode
steps.body: A bridge output is taken between two nodes that both sit near $V_{ex}/2$. The amplifier must respond to the small **difference** $v_d$ and ignore the large **common-mode** voltage $v_{cm}$, the average of the two inputs.

steps.prompt: The two amplifier inputs are at $v_1$ = {{v1|V|5}} and $v_2$ = {{v2|V|5}}.

ask.prompt: Find the differential voltage $v_d = v_1 - v_2$.

steps.title: Common-mode rejection
steps.body: A real differential amplifier gives $v_o = A_d v_d + A_{cm} v_{cm}$. A good one has a tiny common-mode gain $A_{cm}$. The **CMRR** compares the two gains, usually in decibels: 80 dB means the differential gain is 10 000 times the common-mode gain.

steps.prompt: An amplifier has differential gain {{Ad}} and common-mode gain {{Acm}}. Find its CMRR in dB.

steps.title: The instrumentation amplifier
steps.body: The standard solution is the three-op-amp **instrumentation amplifier**: two input buffers (very high input resistance on both inputs) and a difference stage. One gain resistor $R_G$ sets the gain.

steps.prompt: An instrumentation amplifier has $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} and $R_G$ = {{RG|Ω}}. Find its differential gain.
steps.explanation: $G = 1 + \frac{2R_2}{R_G}$ = 1 + 2 × {{R2|Ω}} / {{RG|Ω}} = **{{1+2*R2/RG||4}}**. Changing one resistor changes the gain, and no resistor matching is needed for that.

steps.prompt: In an instrumentation amplifier, a purely common-mode input ($v_1 = v_2$) passes through the first stage (the two input op amps) with a gain of 1, whatever the value of $R_G$.
steps.explanation: With $v_1 = v_2$, both − inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual shorts), so no current flows through $R_G$ and hence none through the $R_2$ resistors. Both buffer outputs simply equal $v_{cm}$. The differential signal, in contrast, is amplified by $1 + 2R_2/R_G$.

steps.prompt: A quarter bridge (one active strain gauge, all four arms nominally equal) is excited with {{Vex|V}}. The gauge has gauge factor {{G}} and is strained by {{u}} µε. Estimate the magnitude of the bridge output.
steps.explanation: $\frac{\Delta R}{R} = G\varepsilon$ = {{G}} × {{u}} × $10^{-6}$ = {{G*u||3}} ppm. Quarter bridge: $|v_{ab}| \approx \frac{V_{ex}}{4}\frac{\Delta R}{R}$ = {{Vex|V}} / 4 × {{G*u*1e-6||3}} = **{{Vex*G*u*1e-6/4|V}}**. Millivolts at most: it must be amplified.

steps.prompt: A platinum RTD $R_{RTD} = R_0(1 + 0.00385\,T)$ is the sensing arm of a bridge whose other three arms equal $R_0$, so it balances at 0 °C. Find $|v_{ab}|$ at $T$ = {{T}} °C.
steps.explanation: $R_{RTD}$ = {{R0*(1+0.00385*T)|Ω|4}}. $v_a = V_{ex}/2$ = {{Vex/2|V}}, $v_b = V_{ex}\frac{R_{RTD}}{R_0 + R_{RTD}}$ = {{v_b|V|4}}. $|v_{ab}|$ = **{{abs(Voc)|V}}**. The small-change estimate $\frac{V_{ex}}{4}\alpha T$ = {{Vex/4*0.00385*T|V}} is noticeably high for large changes: a bridge is not perfectly linear.

steps.prompt: An instrumentation amplifier has $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. Which gain resistor $R_G$ gives a gain of {{G}}?
An amplifier with differential gain {{Ad}} and CMRR = {{C}} dB has a common-mode input of {{vc|V}}. What output voltage does the common-mode input alone produce?
steps.explanation: CMRR = 10^({{C}}/20) = {{10^(C/20)||3}}, so $A_{cm} = A_d/\text{CMRR}$ = {{Ad/10^(C/20)||3}}. Output: $A_{cm}v_{cm}$ = {{Ad/10^(C/20)||3}} × {{vc|V}} = **{{Ad*vc/10^(C/20)|V}}**. Referred to the input that is {{vc/10^(C/20)|V}}, to compare with the wanted $v_d$.

steps.prompt: Difference amplifier with an ideal op amp ($R_3 = R_1$, $R_4 = R_2$). Find $v_o$.
A first-order RC low-pass filter with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{Cc|F}} follows the amplifier.

ask.prompt: By how many dB does it attenuate interference at {{fn|Hz}}? (Give a positive number.)
ask.explanation: $f_c$ = {{1/(2*pi*R*Cc)|Hz}}, so $f/f_c$ = {{fn*2*pi*R*Cc||3}}. Attenuation $= 10\log_{10}\left(1 + (f/f_c)^2\right)$ = **{{10*log10(1+(fn*2*pi*R*Cc)^2)|dB}}** (about 20 dB per decade above $f_c$).

steps.prompt: The magnitude response of a low-pass anti-alias filter is shown. Read its cutoff (−3 dB) frequency.
steps.explanation: Follow the −3 dB line to where it meets the curve and read down: $f_c \approx$ **{{fc|Hz}}**. Above $f_c$ this (second-order) filter falls by 40 dB per decade.

steps.prompt: A single-op-amp difference amplifier built with 10 kΩ input resistors presents a very high input resistance, so a 5 kΩ sensor connected to it is hardly loaded.
steps.explanation: Its input resistance is only of the order of the input resistors (10–20 kΩ), so a 5 kΩ source loses a large fraction of the signal and, worse, unbalances the resistor ratios and ruins the CMRR. That is exactly why instrumentation amplifiers put buffers in front.

steps.prompt: A load cell is a **full** bridge with four active gauges (gauge factor {{G}}), excited with {{Vex|V}}. At rated load the strain is {{u}} µε.

ask.prompt: Find the bridge output at rated load.
ask.explanation: Full bridge: four times the quarter-bridge output, $v_o = V_{ex}G\varepsilon$ = {{Vex|V}} × {{G}} × {{u}} × $10^{-6}$ = **{{Vex*G*u*1e-6|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What amplifier gain makes the rated-load output equal to {{VFS|V}}?
ask.explanation: Bridge output at rated load: $V_{ex}G\varepsilon$ = {{Vex*G*u*1e-6|V}}. Gain = {{VFS|V}} / {{Vex*G*u*1e-6|V}} = **{{VFS/(Vex*G*u*1e-6)||4}}**.

steps.prompt: A quarter bridge (gauge factor 2, excitation {{Vex|V}}) feeds an instrumentation amplifier with $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} and $R_G$ = {{RG|Ω}}. Estimate the magnitude of the amplifier output for a strain of {{u}} µε.

The outputs of a bridge excited by {{Vex|V}} both sit near $V_{ex}/2$. The common-mode error referred to the amplifier input ($v_{cm}/\text{CMRR}$) must stay below {{e|V}}. What minimum CMRR (in dB) does the amplifier need?
A difference amplifier has $R_2/R_1$ = {{K}} and $R_3 = R_1$, but $R_4$ is {{d*100}} % larger than $R_2$ (resistor mismatch). Estimate its CMRR in dB.
steps.explanation: With $v_1 = v_2 = v_{cm}$ the output is $v_{cm}\left[\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}\left(1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1}\right) - \frac{R_2}{R_1}\right]$, so $A_{cm}$ = {{Acm||3}} while $A_d \approx$ {{Ad||4}}. CMRR = 20 $\log_{10}$({{Ad/Acm||3}}) = **{{20*log10(abs(Ad/Acm))|dB}}**. Shortcut: CMRR ≈ $(1 + R_2/R_1)/\delta$ = {{(1+K)/d||3}}. A 1 % resistor can ruin the rejection.

steps.prompt: A thermocouple ($S$ = {{S}} µV/°C, reference at 0 °C) must measure up to {{Tmax}} °C. An instrumentation amplifier with $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} should map {{Tmax}} °C to {{VFS|V}}.

ask.prompt: Which gain resistor $R_G$ gives this gain?

steps.prompt: An ADC samples at {{fs|Hz}}. In front of it sits an order-{{n}} Butterworth anti-alias filter. Set the **highest** cutoff $f_c$ that still attenuates components at $f_s/2$ by at least {{A}} dB (orange point).
steps.explanation: At $f_s/2$ = {{fs/2|Hz}} we need $(f/f_c)^{ {{2*n}} } = 10^{ {{A/10}} } - 1$, so $f_c = \frac{ {{fs/2}} }{ ({{10^(A/10)-1}})^{1/{{2*n}}} }$ = **{{fct|Hz}}**. A higher order lets the cutoff sit much closer to the signal band: with a first-order filter the cutoff would have to be {{(fs/2)/sqrt(10^(A/10)-1)|Hz}}, a fourth-order one allows {{(fs/2)/(10^(A/10)-1)^(1/8)|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: Put the signal path of a strain-gauge weighing system in order
items: Bridge turns ΔR into a millivolt differential signal
Instrumentation amplifier boosts it and rejects the common mode
Low-pass filter removes noise above the signal band
ADC converts the voltage to numbers
steps.explanation: Measurand $\to$ sensor (strain gauges change resistance) $\to$ bridge with excitation (resistance to voltage) $\to$ instrumentation amplifier (gain, CMRR, high input resistance) $\to$ anti-alias low-pass filter $\to$ ADC. Filtering must come **before** sampling, because aliased noise cannot be removed afterwards.

steps.prompt: Tap the **single** resistor you would change to set the gain of this instrumentation amplifier without affecting its common-mode rejection.
steps.explanation: $R_G$ sets the gain $1 + 2R_2/R_G$. A common-mode input drives no current through $R_G$, so changing it does not affect common-mode behaviour. Changing one $R_2$ would unbalance the first stage, and changing one $R$ of the difference stage would directly spoil the CMRR.
